This is Chapter Three, the Danish economy, Episode One: the welfare society and how it grew.
According to the IMF, the International Monetary Fund, Denmark is the world's ninth richest country out of a total of 192 countries, and the third richest of the 27 EU countries.

Gross domestic product, GDP, per inhabitant, that is, the value of the total Danish production over one year divided among each of the country's six million inhabitants, was in 2026 83,000 American dollars, corresponding to just under 540,000 kroner.
But every society has only limited resources, meaning money.
That also applies to rich countries like Denmark.
The word "economy" itself comes from Greek and means "household".
That is, how you manage income and expenses.
That is why economics is also politics.
Because one of the questions that matter most to both the population and the politicians is how the resources should be distributed, and how we make the economy grow.
The Danish economy is often described as a mixed economy.
That means it works within the framework of a private market economy, but that the public sector also plays a big role in the economy.
Some goods and services are produced, bought and sold on the private market, for example food, furniture or taxi rides.
Others, typically services, for example education, hospital treatment or childcare, are offered by the public sector and paid for by taxes and duties.
In addition, the public sector moves a lot of money between citizens, through transfer incomes such as unemployment benefit, cash benefit and pensions.
The private and the public sector depend on each other.
Private business earns money and secures jobs, so that tax is paid, which among other things finances public welfare.

Conversely, the public education system, for example, secures qualified labour for business, while the public health service ensures that companies' employees recover faster and can return after illness, and day-care institutions ensure that children can be looked after so their parents can go to work.
The Finance Act for 2026 is the total budget for the state's expenditure and income.
This chapter describes some overall characteristics of the Danish economy in three areas: the welfare society, business life, and the labour market.
We begin with the welfare society.
The Danish welfare society is built on a principle that the individual citizen has both rights and duties.
Citizens who meet certain conditions have the right to the welfare society's benefits.
But the individual citizen also has a duty to contribute to the community.
Partly by paying tax, partly by working, if you can.
If you are outside the labour market and receive help, you also have a duty to make an active effort yourself to get back to the labour market.
All in all, this way of thinking is an expression of a kind of informal contract between the state and the citizens, with both duties and rights.
The Danish model of the welfare society has many features in common with the other Nordic countries.
People often talk about the Nordic model.
There are also many similarities with other rich countries, but there are some things where the Danish, and Nordic, welfare model stands out.
First: the state has a big responsibility for the citizens' welfare from the cradle to the grave.
There is childcare for all children.
Children and young people have access to free education.
Everyone is guaranteed treatment in case of illness.
There is help or care for the elderly and others who cannot manage on their own.
And there is financial support for those who cannot work and support themselves.
Second: most welfare benefits are financed by the whole population together via taxes and duties.
In many other countries, welfare benefits are mostly financed through social contributions paid by employees and employers.
In Denmark, the right to benefits is normally not dependent on having been in work and having paid social contributions, as is the case in several countries south of Denmark in Europe.
Third: welfare is made available to all citizens when they meet the conditions for receiving it.
Great emphasis is placed on service tasks that relieve the family.
This applies especially to childcare, nurseries, kindergartens and after-school care, and elderly care, home help, nursing homes and so on.
Several European countries have in certain areas been inspired by the Nordic welfare model.
The Danish way of arranging the welfare society makes it possible for both men and women to take an active part in the labour market, even if they have children.
In Danish families with children, both the father and the mother typically work full time or almost full time.
Here too, the European countries have moved in the same direction as the Nordic ones.
Now, how did we get here?
The development of the Danish welfare model.
In all societies, it is the adults who can work who take care of the elderly, of the children, and of those who for one reason or another cannot manage on their own.
Historically, this has often been organised within the individual family or in local communities.
In Denmark, a steadily larger part of these tasks has gradually been taken over by the welfare state.
This has happened by gradually creating a system in which all of society's citizens have a right to get financial and practical help on the basis of uniform criteria.
The first steps towards the welfare society we know today were taken in the 1890s.
It happened in a time of great economic and social change.
Agriculture was reorganised, industry emerged, and the towns grew.
With the changes to the old agricultural and craft society, a number of private social arrangements disappeared.
Instead, the state increasingly began to take care of the citizens who needed help.
More, and gradually more fixed, rules came about for who could be granted social benefits in case of illness, accident, unemployment and old age.
More and more people also got access to the benefits.
In 1933, as part of the so-called Kanslergade Agreement, a major social reform was carried out.
With the reform, 55 social laws were gathered into four people's insurance laws, folkeforsikringslove.
A higher degree of the rights principle was also carried out, that is, clearer rules about when and how much help the individual citizen could get.
Until then, it was largely up to the individual municipality to assess whether a citizen had the right to help, and how much could be given.
The reform also abolished most of the so-called declassification provisions in the social legislation.
That is, it made it the main principle that you could not lose your right to vote or other civil rights because you received help from the public sector.
The Kanslergade Agreement was made in 1933, during the economic crisis of the 1930s, so the problem it was meant to solve was economic.
The most important tracks towards the present welfare society were laid in the 1950s and 1960s.
Several of the fundamental principles of the welfare society were established here.

The social safety net was expanded, among other things with the old-age pension laws in 1956 and 1964, which introduced the old-age pension for all elderly people and not only for the weakest elderly.
So the first old-age pension law came in 1956, and a second followed in 1964.
Previously the state had especially given cash benefits, that is, financial help to citizens who had lost their income due to unemployment, illness and accident, or old age.
But in this period, the welfare society also began to include a number of service benefits, which took over tasks that the family had previously been alone in taking care of.
That applied not least to childcare and home help for the elderly.
The principle of help to the citizen in need was supplemented to a higher and higher degree by a principle that the entire population, rich as well as poor, can benefit from the different benefits.
It was especially from the middle of the 1960s to the end of the 1970s that the big expansion of the service benefits took place.
It happened at the same time as almost all women, also those who were married, came out onto the labour market, so that the stay-at-home housewife almost disappeared.
From 1980 to around the year 2000, this development continued, with the majority of married women going from part-time to full time or almost full time.
It was especially the public sector's takeover of childcare and elderly care and so on that made this possible.
Nearly all children between 1 and 6 years get childcare, while most 7 to 10-year-olds are looked after in an after-school scheme after school.
Maternity and parental leave has also been extended several times, from a very few weeks in the 1970s to the 52 weeks with full unemployment benefit rates that have applied since 2002.

The first old-age pension law came in 1956, and a second in 1964.
The Kanslergade Agreement of 1933 was about the economic crisis.
The big expansion of services was from the mid-1960s to the late 1970s.

This is Chapter Three, Episode Two: pensions, getting people to work, equality, and taxes.
The welfare state depends on the economic development in society.
In the period 1957 to 73 there was strong economic growth.
So the 1960s were years of very high growth, with rising production and consumption and high employment.
The growth in the public sector also continued at a high pace through the 1970s, despite a long economic crisis.
It became more and more clear, however, that the economy had difficulty bearing the development in public expenditure.
So the brakes were put on in the 1980s, and since then growth in public expenditure has continued at a more limited pace, so that it has roughly followed the general growth in the economy.
One of the biggest long-term challenges for the welfare state in Denmark and other European countries is that there are fewer people to pay for the welfare that more people are to enjoy.
That is primarily because life expectancy is rising, but also because the birth rate has been low for many decades.
People therefore speak of the so-called dependency burden, forsørgerbyrde, or the demographic pressure, having risen.
From 1980 to 2026, the share of citizens in Denmark over 64 has grown from 14 percent to 21 percent of the total population.
An important part of the solution has therefore been to extend the working age.
That is, the age at which you are, as a main rule, in the labour market.
The Folketing decided in 2006 that the old-age pension age should be raised as Danes live longer.
The pension age was 65 up to and including 2018, but is gradually being raised: first to 67 in 2022, then to 68 from 2030, and 69 from 2035.
In addition, it was decided in 2011 to shorten the early retirement scheme, efterløn.
Efterløn was introduced in 1979 as a right for people over 60 to withdraw from the labour market before the pension age.
In recent years there has also been a slightly smaller movement in the other direction.
From 2022, people who at 61 have been a long time, 42 to 44 years, in the labour market have got the right to retire one to three years before the old-age pension age.
This is called early pension, tidlig pension.

Early pension is also called the "Arne pension", after the brewery worker Arne Juhl, who became the face of the Social Democrats' election campaign at the general election in 2019 to get the scheme introduced.

The early retirement age was gradually raised from 60 to 62 from 2014 to 2017, and then the period is gradually shortened to 3 years, so that from 2023 you can go on efterløn from the age of 64 to 67.
For most people the benefit also becomes smaller, because the benefit is reduced to a greater extent in relation to how much pension savings the recipient has.

There have also been attempts to get more people into work by shortening the so-called unemployment benefit period, the dagpengeperiode, that is the period in which you can receive support as unemployed from an unemployment insurance fund, an A-kasse.
In 1993 a limit of seven years was set for the unemployment benefit period, and it has been continuously reduced: in 1995 to five years, in 1998 to four years, and since 2010 it has been two years.
At the same time, greater demands are today made to take other work than what you are trained for.

Furthermore, income tax has been lowered for people in work, including with a so-called employment deduction, beskæftigelsesfradrag, that is an amount you do not have to pay tax on if you are in work or have a surplus in your business.
This increases the benefit of being in work, even in jobs with a low wage.
Finally, a number of initiatives have been carried out to get more people into work among the groups that have had difficulty finding work.
It has thus become harder for those who have a lasting and significantly reduced ability to work to get the disability-type early retirement pension, førtidspension.
Instead they have been given the opportunity to work in a so-called flex job, fleksjob, so that they earn a good part themselves and get a public benefit for the rest.
Employment for people with a non-Western immigrant background has also risen overall since 1995, though with large fluctuations in the period.
For example it fell for a number of years after the financial crisis in 2008, and then rose again from 2015 to 16.
But many in this group are still outside the labour market.
In 2024, 68 percent of immigrants with a non-Western background between 25 and 64 were in work, against 83 percent of people of Danish origin in the same age group.
High employment in Denmark contributes to a high level of prosperity, and to Denmark being able to finance an expanded public sector.
The Danish welfare society is characterised by considerable economic redistribution.

This redistribution takes place both through the tax system, because those who earn the most pay the most in tax, and because the welfare state's benefits are given to everyone, and not least to those who are not in work.
Inequality did fall significantly in the period 1945 to 80.
That was especially due to the rapid expansion of the welfare society, large wage increases and long periods of low unemployment.
Inequality has, however, become greater since the 1980s.

This is due, among other things, to the tax system redistributing less from high to low incomes than before, to wage differences having become bigger, and to the value of homes in Copenhagen having grown very quickly over the last 10 to 15 years, which has created bigger differences in wealth.
Denmark still has a relatively high degree of economic equality compared with other countries.
How is it all paid for?
The Danish welfare society is financed through taxes on, for example, income, and through, among other things, VAT, moms, and duties on goods and services.
Moms, VAT, is a duty on goods and services you buy, for example in the shops.
It is not a tax on your income.
Both the state and the municipalities have the right to levy income tax.
Only the state and the municipalities levy income tax: the regions cannot levy taxes.
In 1903, income tax was introduced as a permanent tax.
It was introduced with a markedly lower tax percentage than today.
Income tax means that almost all incomes are taxable, regardless of where they come from.
The Danish income tax is progressive.
That means the percentage you have to pay in tax rises for high incomes.
Thus people with high incomes pay not only a higher amount in tax than people with lower incomes, but also a bigger share of their wage.
Income taxes make up a large part of the taxes in Denmark.

They redistribute more than duties on consumption, for example VAT, because people with lower incomes typically spend a larger share of their wage, which they thereby pay VAT on, while people with a higher income typically save more.
Everyone has a so-called basic deduction, a bundfradrag, an amount on which you do not pay income tax, of the first 54,100 kroner in 2026 that you earn in a year.
On income above the deduction you pay 12 percent in tax to the state and about 25 percent to your municipality.
If you are a member of the national church, folkekirken, you also typically pay about 1 percent church tax.
Church tax is paid only by taxable members of the national church.
Not everyone pays it, and non-members pay no church tax.
In addition, the state collects tax on the highest incomes, so that you pay: a "middle tax", mellemskat, of 7.5 percent on income above 618,400 kroner a year.
A "top tax", topskat, of 15 percent on income above 750,000 kroner a year.
And a "top-top tax", toptopskat, of 20 percent on income above 2.5 million kroner a year.

Early pension, the Arne pension, started in 2022.
The unemployment benefit period was seven years in 1993, five in 1995, four in 1998, and two years since 2010.
In 2024, 68 percent of non-Western immigrants aged 25 to 64 were employed, against 83 percent of people of Danish origin.
Inequality fell from 1945 to 80 and has grown since the 1980s.
Income tax became permanent in 1903, and is progressive.
The 2026 basic deduction is 54,100 kroner; 12 percent goes to the state and about 25 percent to the municipality, plus about 1 percent church tax for members only.
Moms is a duty on goods you buy.
Middle tax is 7.5 percent above 618,400 kroner, top tax 15 percent above 750,000, and top-top tax 20 percent above 2.5 million.

This is Chapter Three, Episode Three: who delivers the welfare society's services.
Who actually provides all this welfare?
The welfare society makes a long list of benefits available to citizens.
It is common to say that the public sector carries out two different kinds of welfare tasks.
First, the public sector helps citizens who find it difficult to manage on their own and therefore need financial help.
About one third of the total public expenditure goes to cash benefits, transfer incomes, to citizens.

They are typically given to people without work and include, among other things, the old-age pension, early retirement pension, the state educational support, SU, maternity benefit, the child and youth benefit, unemployment benefit and sickness benefit, and cash benefit.
But for example families with children also get cash benefits, the child and youth benefit, which is justified by their having greater expenses than families without children or young people at home.
Second, the public sector provides a number of public service benefits to all citizens who need them.
This concerns, for example, nurseries and kindergartens, hospitals, elderly care and many forms of education.
The Folketing and the government lay down the framework for the Danish welfare society through legislation.
But it is especially the 98 municipalities that fill out the framework of the law.
It is the municipalities that in practice deliver most welfare benefits to citizens.
In addition come the regions, which are responsible for running most of the health service.
The regions run the hospitals, sygehusene.
They do not run the police, which is a state task, and not the nurseries, which are a municipal task.
The municipalities act as citizens' main entrance to the public sector.
The municipalities have by far the most of the tasks that are close to the individual citizen.
That applies, among other things, to: childcare in nurseries and kindergartens.
The folkeskoler, the public primary and lower secondary schools.
Libraries and several other cultural tasks.
The effort to get the unemployed into employment, through the municipal jobcentres, which help unemployed citizens get back to work.
Allocation of a long list of social benefits.
And waste collection and other environmental tasks.

The state solves a number of overall tasks such as, for example, the police, the judiciary, that is the courts, domstolene, and defence, as well as tasks such as upper secondary education, gymnasiums and so on, higher education and research.
In connection with the structural reform in 2007, the state also took over all tax collection from the municipalities.
In Denmark, the welfare society is thus as a starting point a public task, carried out by the state, the regions and the municipalities.
But there are others involved as well.
Through the last decades it has become more common to let private companies carry out some of the welfare tasks, however in such a way that it is still the public sector that pays.
In elderly care, the individual can for example freely choose whether they wish to have home help delivered by the municipality or by a private provider.
There is also a strong Danish tradition of involving volunteers in solving welfare tasks.
As the name implies, they make an effort without being paid for it.
Associations and voluntary work are far more widespread in the Nordic countries than in almost all other countries.
They run, among other things, crisis centres, visiting schemes for the elderly, contact and drop-in centres and much more.
It is normally the basic idea that voluntary work should be a supplement to the public service and not a replacement.
It is thus still quite rare for voluntary organisations to be responsible for the basic service.
Voluntary organisations also play a very big role in cultural and leisure life.
That applies not least to sport, where thousands of volunteers act as coaches, for example for children who play football, handball or other sports.
Denmark also has a tradition of so-called free schools, friskoler, which goes all the way back to the middle of the 1800s.
The free schools are owned by an association behind the school, and not by the municipality, and are therefore also often called private schools.
They get a grant from the municipality which corresponds to a high share of the normal expense for a municipal folkeskole.
A smaller part is paid by the parents.
Free schools are found all over the country, and some are very old.
In Denmark, most are run on the basis of a particular educational idea or a wish to have a local school.

Most children still go to municipal folkeskoler, but in recent years there has been a big increase in the share of children who go to free schools or private schools: from about 14 percent in the school year 2008 to 09, to 20 percent in the school year 2024 to 25.
Involvement of parents is also central in Danish schools, kindergartens and nurseries.
For example, there are boards elected by the parents.
There are lots of parent meetings and activities where it is expected that all parents take part.
And in practically all classes, so-called contact parents, kontaktforældre, are elected to organise meetings and get-togethers, and to function as contact to the school board.
This usually goes in turns, so that most parents take part for a period.

Last but not least, the public welfare benefits are supplemented by agreements, collective agreements, overenskomster, between the parties of the labour market, trade unions and employers' organisations.

This applies, for example, to the pension area, where almost everyone today has a so-called labour market pension, arbejdsmarkedspension, which they pay into with a certain percentage of their wage, typically 12 to 17 percent.
The labour market pension is built on top of the old-age pension.
Where the old-age pension is meant to secure all citizens', especially the weakest's, basic needs in old age, the labour market pensions depend on the individual's income as economically active.
For many people with middle incomes or higher incomes, the labour market pension they get paid out is considerably higher than the old-age pension.
In addition to pension, these pension schemes also typically give support in critical illness, and insurance in case of illness and death.
Although not all employees are covered by a collective agreement, it has become the norm for the vast majority of jobs that they have a pension scheme.
Finally, there is also a big private market for pensions, where the individual can save up for their pension in a bank or an insurance company.
Here is your recap for Episode Three.
Public welfare tasks are of two kinds: cash benefits and services.
About one third of public expenditure goes to cash benefits.
The 98 municipalities deliver most welfare services, such as childcare, folkeskoler, elderly care, libraries, getting the unemployed into work, and integration.
The regions run most of the health service, including the hospitals.
The state handles police, the judiciary, defence, upper secondary and higher education, research, and, since the 2007 reform, all tax collection.
Voluntary work supplements, rather than replaces, public service.
Free schools go back to the mid-1800s, and the share of children in free or private schools rose from about 14 percent in 2008 to 09 to 20 percent in 2024 to 25.
A labour market pension is typically 12 to 17 percent of wages and comes on top of the old-age pension.

This is Chapter Three, Episode Four: Danish business life and trade with the rest of the world.
How does a country get from ploughs to pharmaceuticals?

Like most other wealthy countries, Denmark has gradually developed from being an agricultural society to an industrial society, and then, in the last 50 years, to being a so-called knowledge and service society.

That is, we have gone from an economy that is primarily based on the production of goods, to being to a higher degree dependent on highly educated labour, with a focus on using knowledge and getting new ideas, and on the production of services, for example the banking sector, IT support, research or education.
Until the end of the 1800s, the majority of the population worked in agriculture.
But from the 1870s, industry and crafts grew quickly, the population moved from countryside to town, and the towns grew.
Agriculture remained important, however, especially because agricultural goods made up most of Denmark's exports.
The focus was on high-quality animal production, for example meat, butter and cheese, within the framework of the many cooperative associations' dairies and slaughterhouses.
Right up until the end of the 1950s, agricultural goods made up more than half of Denmark's exports.
Agricultural production is still large, but since the 1950s there has been a dramatic increase in efficiency, and today only about two percent of the workforce work in agriculture itself.
But agriculture is still an important export industry.

People often speak in that connection of a food cluster, fødevareklynge, because fewer are employed in agriculture itself and more are employed in processing, transport, sales, marketing and product development.
Agriculture is also changing in other ways.
Agriculture has been criticised for being too efficient in an unfortunate way, among other things because too much poison is used on the fields to kill weeds, fungi and insects.
That has contributed to a beginning green transition, so that Denmark today is the country with the largest share of agriculture, 11.1 percent in 2024, run as organic farming.

Organic farming is run, among other things, without the use of chemical pesticides and artificial fertiliser, and the animals have more room in the stables and better opportunity to get out into the open air.
The first big wave of industrialisation in Denmark took place at the end of the 1800s and the beginning of the 1900s.
Progress continued, but at a somewhat slower pace, until the second big wave of industrialisation, which was from the end of the 1950s to around 1970.
From the beginning of the 1970s, the share of people employed in industry fell, just as had earlier happened in agriculture.
Today, almost four out of five people employed work in private or public service companies, for example in tourism, health, consulting or education.
About 30 percent of employees in Denmark work in the public sector.
That is roughly one third, so most employees, about two thirds, work in the private sector, not the public sector.
The production of agricultural and industrial goods has, however, risen, even though the number of employees has fallen.
That is especially due to the mechanisation of production and the rapid technological development in these sectors.
Denmark has previously been characterised by most companies being small or medium-sized.
That is still true, but more companies have come along that take up a lot of space on the world market in the industries where Denmark is especially strong.

This applies for example to food, where dairies and slaughterhouses are gathered into international giants: Danish Crown was in 2025 the world's second largest pig slaughterhouse, and Arla was in 2025 among the ten largest dairies.
Carlsberg was in 2025 the world's fourth largest brewery.
Denmark has a large pharmaceutical industry.
Several Danish pharmaceutical companies have a large share of the world market, of which Novo Nordisk is the largest.
The location of Novo Nordisk in Denmark is of very great importance for the Danish economy, exports and employment.
Denmark also makes over one third of the world's hearing aids.
The three biggest Danish producers, GN Store Nord, with GN Resound, William Demant, with Oticon, and Widex, are among the biggest hearing aid producers in the world.
In addition, LEGO is one of the world's biggest toy groups.
LEGO was founded in 1932, and is an abbreviation of "leg godt", which means "play well".
The headquarters is in Billund in Jutland.
LEGO is known for making plastic bricks.
Denmark has always been a big seafaring nation and had, in 2024, the world's tenth largest merchant fleet, and the world's second largest container shipping company in 2025, Mærsk.
Add to that companies from the green sector.
The Danish Vestas was in 2024 the world's largest wind turbine producer.
Denmark is also very strong when it comes to energy savings, which can for example be insulation or extra energy-efficient products.
Now to trade with the outside world.
Denmark has a very open economy, where trade with other countries plays a very big role.
Exports make up about half of the country's total production.
That is naturally also because Denmark is a small country, and trade with other countries, not least the neighbouring countries, therefore takes up a lot of space.
Germany is the country Denmark imports, buys, most from, and the USA is the country Denmark exports, sells, most to.
Overall, however, exports to other EU countries are clearly greater than to the USA.
In 2025, Denmark's seven biggest trading partners were the following, in their share of the value of Denmark's total foreign trade, imports and exports.
So measured by total trade, imports plus exports, the USA is now Denmark's biggest trading partner, ahead of Germany.
Germany is still the country Denmark buys most from, the biggest source of imports.
Older exam questions that give Germany as the biggest trading partner are out of date.
Danish governments have in modern times almost always been in favour of as much free trade between countries as possible.
Since the 1990s Denmark has also done better in international competition.
In the same period, Danish exports have in practically all years been higher than imports.
Denmark is a member of a number of international organisations that, like the EU, also work for more free trade.
This applies for example to the OECD, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, and the WTO, the World Trade Organization.
Economic globalisation has brought about big changes on the Danish labour market.
Many companies have moved parts of their production to places in the world where wages are lower.
Not only to China, but also to, for example, Eastern Europe or other European countries.
Up to now, companies have, however, typically kept some important functions in Denmark, for example the development of new products, sales and management.
In return, new big markets have also emerged for Danish products.

This is Chapter Three, the final episode, Episode Five: the Danish labour market.
Most people of working age take part in the Danish labour market.
That applies to both men and women.
In 2024, 76.3 percent of the population, the 16 to 66-year-olds, were employed: 78.4 percent of the men and 74.2 percent of the women.
So about three quarters of Danish women are in work.
The Danish labour market is also characterised by a generally well-educated workforce.
For many years it has been the goal that practically everyone should have an education after the folkeskole, although that has not succeeded quite to the extent that was hoped.
On the other hand, Denmark is one of the countries in the world with the strongest tradition for continuing and further education, that is ongoing education during working life.
Education is also more and more necessary, because many of the jobs that do not require education have been taken over by machines or robots, moved abroad, or simply saved away.
Now to the heart of the matter.
People often talk about a special Danish labour market model, which has roots more than 100 years back in time.
During the early industrialisation at the end of the 1800s, a larger working class gradually emerged in the towns.

The workers joined together in trade unions in the various trades, whose overall main organisation is the Danish Trade Union Confederation, FH, which had the purpose of fighting for better pay and working conditions.
In response, the employers joined together in the Danish Employers' Confederation, which today is called DA.
Several of the principles underlying the Danish labour market come from the September Compromise, Septemberforliget, which the parties of the labour market entered into in 1899.

The compromise is therefore also called "the labour market's constitution", Arbejdsmarkedets Grundlov, and means, among other things, that trade unions and employers' organisations recognise each other as entitled to negotiate on behalf of their members.
The two parties can thus enter into agreements that cover several groups of employers and employees.
Such an agreement is called a collective agreement, an overenskomst.
It typically lays down pay and working conditions.
The September Compromise also establishes that it is the employer who manages and distributes the work, and who can hire and dismiss employees.
Finally, the compromise involves a so-called duty of peace, fredspligt.
That means that a strike, when employees lay down their work, and a lockout, when employers send employees home, are not allowed when a collective agreement has been entered into.
Overall, the Danish labour market model is built on these five central elements.
One: the majority of the workforce is organised in trade unions.
Two: the parties of the labour market themselves agree on pay and working conditions on the labour market, which is called self-regulation.
The state, as a main rule, does not interfere in this, as in certain other countries, unless the parties, after many negotiations, do not seem to be able to agree.
Three: a very large part of the labour market is covered by collective agreements.
Four: there is so-called tripartite cooperation between employees, employers and the state about conditions on the labour market.
And five: there is flexibility and security, flexicurity.
It is thus easy to hire and fire employees in Denmark, but the unemployed also get support from the public sector, which is partly self-paid.
Let's take them one at a time.
First, a high degree of organisation.
On the Danish labour market, the large majority of employees are professionally organised, although the share has fallen in recent decades.
Almost two out of three, 68 percent, of employees were in 2025 members of a trade union.
It is almost only the Nordic countries that have such a high degree of organisation.
The trade union works to secure the members the best possible conditions in the workplaces.
There are trade unions both for privately employed and for publicly employed people.
Both the trade unions and the employers' organisations are gathered in nationwide federations and main organisations.
The biggest main organisation is the Danish Trade Union Confederation, FH.
FH is an umbrella organisation for a total of about 600 trade union federations and organises about 1.3 million members.
DA is the employers' main organisation and organises 11 employers' organisations with about 23,000 companies within, among other things, industry, trade, transport, service and construction.

Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry, with its 23,000 member companies, which employ about 650,000 employees, is Denmark's biggest employers' and business organisation and DA's biggest member organisation.
The second biggest business organisation is Dansk Erhverv, which represents 18,000 companies, which are often smaller than the companies in DI.
There is freedom of association in Denmark.
That means, among other things, that the individual employee decides for themself whether they want to be a member of a trade union, and if so which one.

It also means that it is forbidden for an employer to dismiss an employee because they are a member of a trade union, just as it is forbidden to dismiss an employee because they are not a member of a trade union.
In connection with new hiring, there must also not be a demand that an employee must be a member of a particular trade union.
The state thus does not interfere in pay and working conditions as long as the parties are themselves able to enter into agreements in these areas.
The agreements also cover subjects which in most other countries would be decided by laws passed by parliament and government.
That can be working hours, overtime pay, notice periods or minimum wage.
Denmark thus has no statutory minimum wage, but the agreements between trade unions and employers' organisations in reality have the same effect.
Another example is employees' pension, where the parties of the labour market have agreed a labour market pension on top of the old-age pension that the state pays.
In recent years it has also been agreed that full pay including pension is paid in a larger part of the period when you are on parental leave.
It is also the parties of the labour market themselves who seek to solve the conflicts that may arise.
The basic idea is that the parties of the labour market can adapt agreements faster and better to the individual industry or the individual company.
And when the parties themselves have taken part in making an agreement, they also accept its terms.
More than 80 percent of the Danish labour market is covered by collective agreements.

A collective agreement is an agreement between a trade union and an employer or employers' organisation about pay and working conditions within a particular area, which the parties themselves delimit in the agreement.
An employer who has entered into a collective agreement is obliged to give all the employees the pay and working conditions which appear from the agreement.
That applies, for example, to agreements about pay, pension, working hours, holiday and notice.
If the parties do not agree on a new collective agreement when an existing agreement expires, there will be a conflict on the labour market.
That is, the employees strike, or the employer can lock out their employees, send them home from work without pay.
To avert conflicts on the labour market, the state has since 1910 had a so-called Conciliation Institution, Forligsinstitutionen, which is often referred to as "the conciliator", forligsmanden.

The conciliator can, if there is a prospect of conflict between the parties of the labour market, for example summon the parties to negotiations or put forward a so-called mediation proposal, a mæglingsforslag, which is a proposal for a settlement, a compromise, between the parties.
The conciliator can also postpone a threatening labour market conflict, typically by a couple of weeks.
It happens relatively rarely that there is a major conflict on the labour market, but it has happened several times.
The last time there was a major conflict on the private labour market was in 1998.
It meant, for example, that many buses did not run and that the shops did not get goods delivered.

The government and the Folketing have then typically, as they also did in 1998, relatively quickly made a law about a collective agreement, so that the employees return to work and the situation becomes normal again.
In those cases, the Folketing's law has always been based on a mediation proposal which the conciliator on the labour market has put forward.
In that connection, people speak of "raising a mediation outline to law".
Third, and finally, tripartite cooperation and flexicurity.
The state also typically cooperates continuously with the parties of the labour market about shaping the part of the labour market policy that is laid down through legislation.
This applies, for example, to rules about the working environment, job placement, labour market training and unemployment insurance.
This cooperation is called tripartite cooperation, trepartssamarbejde, because it consists of three parties: the state, the employers and the employees.
The cooperation is meant to ensure a labour market that is both flexible for employers and secure for employees.
The flexibility consists of it being relatively easy for employers to dismiss employees when the economy is bad, and to hire employees when things go well.
The security consists of employees having an economic security in the form of unemployment support if they lose their job.
This also makes it less risky to change jobs.
Employees are also secured help to get back to the labour market, for example through education, internships or other activation.
This combination of flexibility and security is often referred to as the Danish flexicurity model.

In 2024, 76.3 percent of 16 to 66-year-olds were employed: 78.4 percent of men and 74.2 percent of women.
The labour market model has roots more than 100 years back and rests on the September Compromise of 1899, the labour market's constitution.
Strikes and lockouts are not allowed under a collective agreement, the duty of peace.
The five elements are: high organisation, self-regulation, collective agreements, tripartite cooperation and flexicurity.
In 2025, 68 percent of employees were union members.
FH has about 600 federations and 1.3 million members.
DA has 11 organisations and about 23,000 companies.
DI has 23,000 companies and 650,000 employees; Dansk Erhverv 18,000 companies.
There is freedom of association, and no statutory minimum wage.
More than 80 percent of the labour market is covered by collective agreements.
The conciliator, from 1910, can summon negotiations, propose mediation and postpone a conflict by a couple of weeks.
The last major conflict on the private labour market was in 1998, and the Folketing made a law based on the mediation proposal.
Tripartite cooperation involves the state, employers and employees.
Flexicurity means it is easy to hire and fire, with unemployment support for those who lose their job.
